# Overlap + reorder: design competition (owner-refined 2026-09-13)

Mainline (Fable) plans and judges. Codex gpt-6 max codes, one lane per FORK, own worktree from
origin/cpp. Mainline gates, measures, merges the winner, deletes the rest. No mainline source edits.

## Structure: compete on forks, share everything else

Most of what could be built does not conflict. Competing lanes that differ in three unrelated ways
cannot tell you which difference won. So:

  * A FORK is a genuine either/or -- two mechanisms that cannot both be true of the same code path.
    One lane per side. The competition decides the fork.
  * A SHARED MECHANISM is something every design could benefit from and nothing forbids. EVERY lane
    builds it, the same way, so the fork is measured against a common floor.
  * A CONSTRAINT is a property every design must satisfy; it is judged, not optional.

### Forks (these are what the competition decides)
  F1  OVERLAP TARGET: stage idleness (O1) vs cache residency (O2).
      O1 fills idle stage time by pipelining parse/exec/reply across batches -- the historical 2s
      "iofused" design (+10.6% at p8). O2 sizes the in-flight working set to the cache (window
      derived from measured L1d/L2, never a constant) so prefetched data is resident when each
      stage needs it. They disagree about WHY p32 hits a ceiling: O1 predicts it cannot help at
      p32 (batches full, nothing idle); O2 predicts it can (the stall is residency, not idleness).
      The p32 cells decide this fork, and the loser's prediction is a result either way.
  F2  REORDER TRIGGER: promote past a blocker (R1) vs reorder only across cost classes (R2).
      R1 promotes short commands past a long one within the scope -- the recorded -12-14% p99.9
      with a -2% GET tax. R2 runs the scheduler only when a batch mixes static cost classes; a
      uniform batch takes the untouched fast path. They disagree about whether the GET tax is
      inherent to reordering or an artefact of running the scheduler on batches with nothing to
      reorder. Pure-GET p32 in both modes decides this fork.

### Shared mechanisms (every lane builds these, identically)
  S1  Zero-bookkeeping discipline (was O3): no per-op counters, no per-op indirection added by the
      schedule; overlap/reorder decisions are per-BATCH branches. Report instr/op delta; the target
      is zero. This is the recorded failure mode of this family and every lane must be immune to it.
  S2  Mode reporting (was O4): every design measured in 1s AND 2s and reports both. If a design
      helps 2s and hurts 1s, its 1s arm must be a documented no-op -- not a loss shipped because the
      2s number looked good. The history says exactly this asymmetry exists; every lane confirms or
      refutes it on the current tree.
  S3  Scope instrumentation (was R3): before reordering, measure where long commands actually sit
      relative to the reorder point in both modes (last week's finding: the static predictor misses
      several slow shapes and the blockers may not be inside the scope at all). Both reorder lanes
      run the same instrumentation and report it; if it says the scope is wrong, that is the
      result and both lanes report it.
  S4  Amortization study per mechanism (owner requirement). For EVERY small mechanism a lane adds:
        fixed cost      -- what it costs when it does nothing (the 0-knob path must allocate and
                           execute nothing; measure that it does not);
        per-op cost     -- instructions added on the hot path when armed, counted not guessed;
        payoff          -- measured cycles/op improvement in the regime it targets;
        break-even      -- the load/depth/mix at which payoff exceeds cost, as a number.
      A mechanism whose break-even lies outside any regime we run is deleted, not shipped off.
      This is the [[thredis-lb-3pct-budget]] rule applied per mechanism rather than per feature.

### Constraints (judged; a design that violates one loses)
  C1  cycles/op = instr/op / IPC is the verdict. IPC alone is never accepted.
  C2  Affinity: measured with read-local, atomics, key-lb, client-lb ARMED, in both modes. A design
      that wins isolated and loses armed loses.
  C3  Decomposition: multi-piece designs measured piece by piece as well as bundled.
  C4  Zero regression on GET/SET/MGET/MSET at p1 and p32 in both modes.

## Knobs: free during development, collapsed at the end
Lanes MAY add knobs while coding and testing -- a per-mechanism on/off is how S4's amortization is
measured, and a window-size knob is how O2 finds its window. The END STATE is the current surface
only: --overlap 0|1 and --reorder 0|1, where 0 allocates nothing and 1 is the best configuration
the measurements chose. Every development knob is collapsed by hardcode-or-delete before merge: a
mechanism that measured as a consistent win is hardcoded on, one that did not is deleted, and a
tunable is fixed at its measured optimum or derived at runtime -- never left as a knob. The lane's
report must show the collapse: which knobs existed, what each measured, and what each became.

## Cells that decide it
The gate's 17 smoke cells, plus p8 GET/SET in both modes (overlap's historical sweet spot), the 8:2
tail cells with reorder off/on (t01-t06), and one 2048-connection cell (the recorded reversal).
Cycles/op read from the ABBA run's perf counters; rate at matched load alongside.

## Lanes
  overlap-O1  stage-idle       (F1 side A) + S1 S2 S4
  overlap-O2  cache-budgeted   (F1 side B) + S1 S2 S4
  reorder-R1  head-promotion   (F2 side A) + S1 S2 S3 S4
  reorder-R2  cost-class       (F2 side B) + S1 S2 S3 S4
Four lanes, not seven. Each gets this file, HISTORY-overlap-reorder.md, and the judging rules.
Lanes code freely; the box is scheduled by mainline, one measuring lane at a time.

# Cache competition (owner addition 2026-09-13)

## What already exists -- do not rediscover it
The cache-utilisation audit (cx-cacheutil, CACHEUTIL.md, 2026-09-10) got as far as a ranked
candidate list with predictions recorded BEFORE measurement, IBS demand-miss attribution across all
12 workers, a source-derived hot/cold field map for Op/Client/ROB/ThreadCtx/Shard/FlatStore, and one
isolated PRE/POST: candidate 1 (move the every-command `total_commands_` store off the ThreadCtx
line that peers read) measured cycles/op -3.36% on 1s GET p32, IPC +3.9%, instr/op +0.4% -- triage
grade (box was shared). It never reached a verdict because its measurement window kept being
contended. That table is the starting point; the audit's own words: "these are sampled-demand
rankings, not an additive allocation of all fills/op". Two recorded laws govern this work:
  * COHERENCE NOT-HIDING: load stalls hide behind other work at saturation; producer STORES into
    lines a consumer reads (RFO) do not. Rank candidates by RFOs removed, not misses removed.
  * LAYOUT SENSITIVITY: pure code placement moves a 2s GET cell +-0.7%; a sub-1% claim needs a
    padding control. Layout locks (Op 336, Client 1984, ThreadCtx 1408, Shard 1440, FlatStore 944,
    Rob<64> 192, AtomicEntry 144) must hold or be re-locked with a stated reason.

## Structure: one fork, shared mechanisms, same judging

### Fork
  F3  WHERE THE CACHE IS LOST: layout (L1) vs access pattern (L2).
      L1 says the hot structures are laid out badly -- hot and cold fields share lines, an every-op
      store sits on a peer-read line, Op/Client headers straddle -- and the fix is packing: the
      audit's candidates 1, 2, 3 and 5, taken as far as the layout locks allow, each measured
      alone (C3) and ranked by RFOs removed. L2 says layout is secondary and the loss is in WHICH
      lines a stage touches and WHEN -- so the fix is access ordering: touch a structure's lines in
      one pass per stage, hoist the per-op reads of ThreadCtx/Shard out of the per-op loop into
      per-batch locals, and prefetch to a measured window (this is where it meets overlap O2). They
      disagree about whether fills/op falls more from moving fields or from moving code. Both must
      report fills/op AND RFOs/op AND cycles/op; the fork is decided on cycles/op with the others
      as explanation.

### Shared mechanisms (both lanes)
  S5  RFO ranking. Every candidate is ranked by producer-stores-into-consumer-lines removed, from
      IBS, before any is built. A candidate that removes only load misses is deprioritised: at
      saturation those hide.
  S6  Padding control. Every layout or placement change ships with a pad-only twin -- same size
      change, no field moved -- so a +-0.7% placement artefact cannot be reported as a win.
  S7  Locks stay locked. sizeof static_asserts hold; a change that needs a lock moved states the
      new size and why, and the gate's footprint row must agree.
  S4  Amortization per mechanism, as above -- for cache work the "fixed cost" is footprint growth
      and the "per-op cost" is any added indirection; a sidecar that saves a line but adds a
      pointer chase must show the chase is cheaper than the line.

### Constraints: C1-C4 apply unchanged. The cell that most often flips sign on cache changes is 2s
GET p32 (recorded), so it is mandatory in both arms.

### Lanes
  cache-L1  layout    (F3 side A) + S4 S5 S6 S7
  cache-L2  access    (F3 side B) + S4 S5 S6 S7
Both start from the audit's candidate table and IBS data in cx-cacheutil/, not from scratch. Both
must first REPRODUCE candidate 1's -3.36% on a quiet box at confirmation grade -- if it does not
reproduce, the audit's attribution is suspect and both lanes say so before building anything else.

## Interaction with overlap
O2 (cache-budgeted overlap) and L2 (access ordering) share a mechanism -- prefetch to a measured
window. They are built in different lanes on purpose: O2 asks whether overlap's p32 ceiling is
residency; L2 asks whether the steady-state working set is touched efficiently. If both win, the
merge is one mechanism, not two; if one wins and the other loses, that tells us which question was
the real one. Mainline reconciles at merge time; the lanes do not coordinate.

## All six lanes
  overlap-O1  overlap-O2  reorder-R1  reorder-R2  cache-L1  cache-L2
Six codex lanes, six worktrees, coding in parallel; the box is scheduled one measuring lane at a
time by mainline. Merge order after judging: cache first (it changes the floor the other two are
measured against), then overlap, then reorder, then coadapt.

# Expanded design space (owner request 2026-09-13: "there ought to be a lot more ways")

The first round named only the designs the history had already tried. Reading the code (ex_loop.h)
shows the real structure and where the unexplored room is:
  * Overlap today is ONE fixed rotation -- fused_pass_impl<PipelineBatch> with a "three-way" turn
    that inserts a single independent filler into the first batch's prefetch gap. Nothing is
    staged across a call ("the batch remains the stack-local whole batch"). Batch = kExecBatch,
    a power of two <= 32. The io->ex->io crossing is one handoff Ring.
  * Reorder today is a STATIC length-class bucket sort (kExSchedClasses x kRobWindow = 192 buckets)
    run once per gathered batch, BEFORE prefetch so prefetch order matches execution order, with
    every special task a hard FIFO barrier.
Both are single points in a much larger space. The new forks below are genuinely mutually
exclusive with each other AND with F1-F3; everything they share stays shared (S1-S7).

## Overlap: four more forks
  F4  WHAT IS OVERLAPPED WITH WHAT. Today: the ex stage's storage prefetch overlaps one filler.
      O5  IO-EX SOFTWARE PIPELINE: parse batch N+1 on the io side WHILE ex executes batch N while
          io writes back batch N-1 -- a true 3-stage pipeline with a stage per batch in flight,
          not one filler in one gap. Needs one batch of state staged across the call (today
          nothing is). Win condition: stage utilisation at p8-p32; cost: the staging buffer's
          footprint and the per-batch handoff.
      O6  INTRA-BATCH SPLIT: split a gathered batch in two halves; execute half A while
          prefetching half B, then swap -- overlap INSIDE the ex stage with zero cross-stage
          staging. Cheapest possible overlap; its ceiling is half a batch of hidden latency.
      O7  OVERLAP THE REPLY SIDE: today the filler hides storage prefetch. Hide the WRITEBACK
          instead -- serialise batch N's replies while executing batch N+1. The history says the
          2s ceiling is the hand-off (~25M flat = hand-off bound), so the reply crossing may be
          the real bottleneck at p32, not the store.
  F5  BATCH SHAPE. Today: fixed power-of-two <= 32, one size for every depth.
      O8  ADAPTIVE BATCH DEPTH: size the gathered batch from the observed arrival depth (memtier
          pipeline depth is endogenous -- recorded) rather than a constant. Deep pipes get big
          batches (amortise the hand-off), shallow pipes get small ones (latency). Derived at
          runtime from a window, never a knob ([[thredis-knob-philosophy]]: -1 = auto).
      O9  TWO-TIER BATCH: a small hot batch that executes immediately plus a large prefetch
          horizon that only issues prefetches -- decouple "how many to execute now" from "how far
          ahead to warm the cache". This is O2's window idea taken to its conclusion: the horizon
          is sized to the cache, the batch to the hand-off.
  F6  WHO DRIVES. Today the ex loop pulls.
      O10 IO-SIDE ISSUE: the io thread issues the storage prefetch for a batch at parse time
          (it already has the key), so by the time ex dequeues it the line is resident. Moves
          the prefetch to the thread that has the key earliest. Risk: prefetch into the wrong
          core's cache in 2s (io and ex are different cores) -- so this may be a 1s-only win,
          which S2 will show.
  F7  1s SPECIFIC. The history says 1s LOSES with overlap (-19.7/-28.0/-14.6%) and goes idle.
      O11 1s LOCAL-READ-AWARE ROTATION: in 1s the same thread parses, executes AND serves lane
          reads. Today's rotation was designed for 2s and grafted on. Design the 1s rotation
          from scratch around the read-local lane: lane drain / owner exec / parse as three
          explicit phases with the lane getting the prefetch gap. Win condition: 1s stops losing.

## Reorder: four more forks
  F8  WHAT DRIVES THE ORDER. Today: static length class.
      R4  MEASURED-COST CLASSES: replace the static class with a per-command running cost estimate
          (EWMA of observed service time per command id, sampled at a window, not per op). Last
          week found the static predictor misses several slow shapes; this learns them. Cost: one
          table lookup per op -- S4 must show it pays.
      R5  DEADLINE / AGE ORDER: order by how long each op has ALREADY waited (arrival stamp),
          not by predicted cost. Bounds tail latency directly rather than inferring it; a long
          blocker that arrived first still goes first, so this is a different trade from R1.
  F9  WHERE THE REORDER HAPPENS. Today: once, per gathered ex batch, before prefetch.
      R6  IO-SIDE ADMISSION ORDER: reorder at parse time across the io thread's connections,
          before the hand-off, so the ex batch ARRIVES in cost order and ex never runs a
          scheduler. Moves the work to the stage with the most slack.
      R7  CONTINUOUS TWO-QUEUE: instead of sorting each batch, keep two ex queues (short / long)
          and interleave them with a ratio -- no per-batch sort at all, a queue pick per op.
          Cheaper than a 192-bucket sort; the question is whether coarse two-class is enough.
  F10 WHAT MOVES. Today: whole tasks move within a batch; specials are barriers.
      R8  BLOCKER SPLITTING: instead of reordering AROUND a long command, split the long command
          itself into resumable slices (BITCOUNT over N bytes -> k slices) so it never blocks a
          batch for its full cost. Removes the need to reorder for the commands it applies to.
          Correctness-heavy (RYOW, atomic groups); S3 says which commands are actually long.

## Cache: three more forks
  F11 WHAT TO PLACE. Today: the audit ranked field moves within existing structs.
      L3  PER-STAGE STRUCT SPLIT: split Op/Client into a hot header touched by every stage and
          a cold body touched by one, so each stage's working set is a set of contiguous lines --
          the audit's candidate 5 (sidecar) generalised. Trades a pointer chase for a line; S4
          decides.
  F12 WHERE THINGS LIVE. Today: allocation is by class; core-of-birth is whatever ran the alloc.
      L4  OWNER-LOCAL ARENAS: allocate a shard's records from an arena on the shard owner's
          core/CCX so producer and consumer share an L3 slice (this box: 16 L3 domains, 8c each;
          connalloc was shelved for putting the record on the WRONG core -- this puts it on the
          right one by construction). Measured by REMOTE fills/op, which the audit records.
  F13 WHEN LINES ARE TOUCHED. Today: a batch touches what it touches.
      L5  COHERENCE SCHEDULING: from the RFO ranking (S5), find the producer stores that land in
          consumer-read lines and BATCH them -- accumulate per-op counters in a thread-local and
          publish once per batch, so the RFO happens 1/32 as often. This is candidate 1's idea
          made systematic: every hot-line store, not one.

## Lane count and scheduling
  Round 1 (running): O1 O2 | R1 R2 | L1 L2                                    = 6 lanes
  Round 2 (this):    O5 O6 O7 O8 O9 O10 O11 | R4 R5 R6 R7 R8 | L3 L4 L5      = 15 lanes
Twenty-one lanes total. They CODE in parallel (cores 112-127 are enough for compiling); they
MEASURE one at a time, and the box is the constraint: at ~35 min per ABBA smoke run, 21 candidates
is ~12 hours of measurement. Mainline schedules it; the order is by cheapest-to-decide first (O6,
R7, L5 are small) so losers are eliminated early and the box goes to the contenders.

## Judging additions for the expanded field
  * A design that duplicates a shared mechanism another lane already built REUSES it, it does not
    rebuild it; mainline will merge shared mechanisms first and rebase the field onto them.
  * Every fork's LOSER writes down its prediction and why it lost; that is data, not waste. F1's
    loser settles the residency question; F8's loser settles whether cost can be predicted at all.
  * Pairs that turn out compatible (O9 + O2, R6 + R2, L4 + L5) are noted for a COMBINATION round
    after judging -- the combination is built by one lane from the merged winners and measured
    against each alone (C3: bundles have sign-flipped component-wise here before).

# TomoKV — project context for codex

Prepend this to every codex prompt. It is the shared background; each prompt then states its own scope.
Written 2026-09-07. Baseline commit `78c3e5391` (`origin/cpp`), full gate 344/344.

## What it is

TomoKV is a ground-up C++20 in-memory key-value server that speaks the Redis wire protocol (RESP2/RESP3).
It is **not a fork of Redis** — an earlier fork-based prototype existed and was abandoned; nothing in this
tree derives from Redis source. It implements **243 registered commands**. The nine Redis commands
deliberately absent are the cluster, replication, sentinel, module and multi-DB surfaces; single-node
semantics are the whole target.

It is a research system. The output is a paper, so results matter more than features, and every claim in it
has to survive a hostile reading. Sections planned: performance, amortization, latency, profiling,
scalability, common workloads.

## Architecture

**Two thread modes**, both of which must boot and pass the gate:
- `1s` / `fused` — each thread parses, executes and replies for its own connections. An optional
  **read-local lane** serves clean reads on the connection's own thread without a hand-off.
- `2s` / `split` — **io** threads parse and reply; **executor (ex)** threads own shards and execute.
  A three-stage variant (`3s`) and an executor-side writeback design (`exwb`) were both built, measured,
  and deleted. Do not propose either.

**Sharding and ownership.** Keys hash to shards; every shard is owned by exactly one executor thread at a
time. Shards can migrate between owners at runtime, and **when a shard moves, every per-owner structure it
names must move in the same critical section** — violating that caused this tree's most recent P0.

**Ordering ring (`rob`).** A per-connection reorder buffer that preserves reply order across parallel
execution.

**Atomics.** Multi-key atomicity uses group-scoped epoch-MVCC. Cross-shard commands use scatter-gather.
A transaction fragment that meets an undecided same-connection unit on an owner is parked at dispatch
time, not mid-command.

**Flip.** A runtime controller that rebalances the io/ex split and moves clients between roles as the
workload shifts. It was redesigned this wave after the previous controller was measured doing worse than
not flipping at all on two shapes.

**Load balancing.** Key-affine and client-affine balancing (`--key-lb`, `--client-lb`), both default on.

Networking is io_uring; the allocator is jemalloc.

## Non-negotiable correctness laws

Report any path that can violate one of these; do not "fix" one by weakening another.
- Single-owner writes.
- Reads are never obstructed by writes: immutable replacement plus QSBR. **No reader retries and no
  seqlocks on the per-operation path.**
- In-place overwrite is banned while the read-local lane is armed.
- Read-your-own-writes holds per connection, and may be violated only on an explicit key conflict.
- Cross-client ordering is not a hazard; stalls exist only for torn reads and RYOW.
- Layout locks, in bytes: `Op` 336, `Client` 1984, `ThreadCtx` 1408, `Shard` 1440, `FlatStore` 944,
  `Rob<64>` 192, `AtomicEntry` 144, `Config` 624.
- Both thread modes boot. Main commands carry zero regression. One file per feature.

## The box

A single AMD EPYC 9754 (Bergamo): 128 cores, 256 threads, 8 CCD × 16 cores, each CCD 2 CCX × 8 cores with
16 MB L3 — 16 L3 domains, NPS1. Measured node optimum is 8 cores, one CCX. Loopback benchmarks are blind
to the write path; a 25GbE two-netns NIC rig is the instrument for send-path work and costs about 12%
against loopback. Box noise is ±0.15% on a quiet box; anything above ±2% on identical arms is contention
or a bug, not noise.

**The gate boots nothing like a default server.** `tests/gate.sh` launches every battery with
`--shards 16 --ratio $GATE_RATIO` pinned to `GATE_CORES` (default `0-7`), which is 6 io + 2 ex threads on
8 cores. Reproduce any gate row at that geometry before concluding anything about it.

## What it is measured against

Redis 7.4 and 8.8.1, Dragonfly 1.40.2, KeyDB, Microsoft Garnet (net10.0), memcached 1.6.45, plus YCSB
0.17.0 traces. Binaries and digests: `/home/user/Projects/bench-bins/MANIFEST.md`.

We do not win everywhere and the paper will not claim we do. At 64 real cores and pipeline depth 128,
Garnet reaches 62.8M ops/s against our 34.4M. We hold depth 1, where we reach 4.35M. Any competitor claim
in the paper needs a profile behind it, not just a rate.

## How performance is judged

**cycles/op = instructions/op ÷ IPC.** Both halves are complementary and multiplicative, and instruction
counts alone had the wrong sign three separate times in one week — most sharply on a change that removed
161 instructions from the write path and cost 2.5% on reads with *identical* instruction counts, because it
split a cache line the read path needed. Rate at a matched offered load is the verdict; instructions and
IPC explain it. Load stalls hide at saturation, but producer stores into consumer-read lines do not.

Every optimization lands with a PRE vs POST table. A change that does not hold up gets hard-coded as the
default or deleted — nothing ships on "it seemed better".

## Why this work looks the way it does

Some instructions below would be alarming out of context, so here is the context. This is a single-user
research box. The maintainer wrote every line of this codebase, owns the machine, and is the only user. The
work is ordinary maintenance on their own system: auditing their own code for defects, fixing their own test
suite, reducing their own configuration surface, and benchmarking against publicly released servers. Nothing
here touches anyone else's data, systems or accounts.

Four specifics that read oddly without the reason:

1. **"Never run the server, the benchmark or the gate."** This is about measurement integrity and nothing
   else. Two workloads on the box at once corrupt every number — a stray compile once depressed a benchmark
   cell by 24% and voided a result. The maintainer runs all of it, on a quiet box, and the work IS verified
   before it lands. You are being asked to produce a diff, not to skip verification.

2. **"Never edit `EXPECT_QUICK` / `EXPECT_FULL`."** Those constants are how many test rows must pass. Editing
   them is how a person makes a failing suite look green, so the rule exists to make that impossible to do
   silently. It is a stricter standard than normal, not a looser one. State what the count should become and
   why; the maintainer changes it.

3. **Concurrency vocabulary.** This is a database. "Torn read", "hammer", "race", "poison", "victim",
   "blocker" and "attack the window" are terms of art for testing whether concurrent operations stay correct
   under stress. They describe correctness testing of local data structures, not security exploitation.

4. **Deliberately breaking a mechanism to check a test.** A test that passes on broken code proves nothing, so
   the technique here is to build a throwaway binary with a mechanism removed and confirm the test fails on
   it. That build is never committed and never runs outside the box. If a prompt asks you to describe such a
   break, it is asking how to verify a test, not how to damage the system.

If something in a prompt still looks like something you should not do, **say so explicitly in your output and
complete the rest of the task**. A stated objection is useful. Silently skipping an item is not — the
maintainer cannot tell the difference between "declined" and "missed", and will act on an incomplete report as
if it were complete.

## Working rules for codex

- **Never run a server, a benchmark, or the gate.** The maintainer runs the box. Report, or produce a diff.
- Edit only inside your own worktree.
- Never edit `EXPECT_QUICK` / `EXPECT_FULL` in `tests/gate.sh`. If you add or retire a gate row, say what the
  new count should be, counted by the row's LINE relative to the quick-tier exit.
- Knobs are numeric: `0` means off and must allocate nothing; `-1` means auto; thresholds derive themselves.
  Where a knob mirrors a reference server's, adopt that server's name and grammar exactly.
- A test that cannot fail proves nothing. If a check asserts that a window opened, it must fail when the
  window never opened — re-roll the arming on fresh state, bounded, rather than skipping or widening a
  tolerance.

## Closed doors — measured, negative, do not re-propose

`3s` three-stage mode; `exwb` executor-side writeback (−11 to −22%); AMAC and any CR/MR split (the only
boundary is io/ex); reorder-and-window; seqlocks on the per-op path; connection-side record allocation
(`connalloc`, cycles flat, record born on the wrong core); executor-major task collapse (`exmajor`,
−2 to −3%); the read-local capacity hand-off line split (`t-pubdiet`, +1.97% SET but −2.50% GET).

The maintainer PLANS, TESTS, GATES and MERGES. Codex lanes CODE. A lane may build and run its own

Feature lanes run as DESIGN COMPETITIONS: see /home/user/Projects/COMPETITION-overlap-reorder.md

# Overlap + reorder: design competition (owner-refined 2026-09-13)

Mainline (Fable) plans and judges. Codex gpt-6 max codes, one lane per FORK, own worktree from
origin/cpp. Mainline gates, measures, merges the winner, deletes the rest. No mainline source edits.

## Structure: compete on forks, share everything else

Most of what could be built does not conflict. Competing lanes that differ in three unrelated ways
cannot tell you which difference won. So:

  * A FORK is a genuine either/or -- two mechanisms that cannot both be true of the same code path.
    One lane per side. The competition decides the fork.
  * A SHARED MECHANISM is something every design could benefit from and nothing forbids. EVERY lane
    builds it, the same way, so the fork is measured against a common floor.
  * A CONSTRAINT is a property every design must satisfy; it is judged, not optional.

### Forks (these are what the competition decides)
  F1  OVERLAP TARGET: stage idleness (O1) vs cache residency (O2).
      O1 fills idle stage time by pipelining parse/exec/reply across batches -- the historical 2s
      "iofused" design (+10.6% at p8). O2 sizes the in-flight working set to the cache (window
      derived from measured L1d/L2, never a constant) so prefetched data is resident when each
      stage needs it. They disagree about WHY p32 hits a ceiling: O1 predicts it cannot help at
      p32 (batches full, nothing idle); O2 predicts it can (the stall is residency, not idleness).
      The p32 cells decide this fork, and the loser's prediction is a result either way.
  F2  REORDER TRIGGER: promote past a blocker (R1) vs reorder only across cost classes (R2).
      R1 promotes short commands past a long one within the scope -- the recorded -12-14% p99.9
      with a -2% GET tax. R2 runs the scheduler only when a batch mixes static cost classes; a
      uniform batch takes the untouched fast path. They disagree about whether the GET tax is
      inherent to reordering or an artefact of running the scheduler on batches with nothing to
      reorder. Pure-GET p32 in both modes decides this fork.

### Shared mechanisms (every lane builds these, identically)
  S1  Zero-bookkeeping discipline (was O3): no per-op counters, no per-op indirection added by the
      schedule; overlap/reorder decisions are per-BATCH branches. Report instr/op delta; the target
      is zero. This is the recorded failure mode of this family and every lane must be immune to it.
  S2  Mode reporting (was O4): every design measured in 1s AND 2s and reports both. If a design
      helps 2s and hurts 1s, its 1s arm must be a documented no-op -- not a loss shipped because the
      2s number looked good. The history says exactly this asymmetry exists; every lane confirms or
      refutes it on the current tree.
  S3  Scope instrumentation (was R3): before reordering, measure where long commands actually sit
      relative to the reorder point in both modes (last week's finding: the static predictor misses
      several slow shapes and the blockers may not be inside the scope at all). Both reorder lanes
      run the same instrumentation and report it; if it says the scope is wrong, that is the
      result and both lanes report it.
  S4  Amortization study per mechanism (owner requirement). For EVERY small mechanism a lane adds:
        fixed cost      -- what it costs when it does nothing (the 0-knob path must allocate and
                           execute nothing; measure that it does not);
        per-op cost     -- instructions added on the hot path when armed, counted not guessed;
        payoff          -- measured cycles/op improvement in the regime it targets;
        break-even      -- the load/depth/mix at which payoff exceeds cost, as a number.
      A mechanism whose break-even lies outside any regime we run is deleted, not shipped off.
      This is the [[thredis-lb-3pct-budget]] rule applied per mechanism rather than per feature.

### Constraints (judged; a design that violates one loses)
  C1  cycles/op = instr/op / IPC is the verdict. IPC alone is never accepted.
  C2  Affinity: measured with read-local, atomics, key-lb, client-lb ARMED, in both modes. A design
      that wins isolated and loses armed loses.
  C3  Decomposition: multi-piece designs measured piece by piece as well as bundled.
  C4  Zero regression on GET/SET/MGET/MSET at p1 and p32 in both modes.

## Knobs: free during development, collapsed at the end
Lanes MAY add knobs while coding and testing -- a per-mechanism on/off is how S4's amortization is
measured, and a window-size knob is how O2 finds its window. The END STATE is the current surface
only: --overlap 0|1 and --reorder 0|1, where 0 allocates nothing and 1 is the best configuration
the measurements chose. Every development knob is collapsed by hardcode-or-delete before merge: a
mechanism that measured as a consistent win is hardcoded on, one that did not is deleted, and a
tunable is fixed at its measured optimum or derived at runtime -- never left as a knob. The lane's
report must show the collapse: which knobs existed, what each measured, and what each became.

## Cells that decide it
The gate's 17 smoke cells, plus p8 GET/SET in both modes (overlap's historical sweet spot), the 8:2
tail cells with reorder off/on (t01-t06), and one 2048-connection cell (the recorded reversal).
Cycles/op read from the ABBA run's perf counters; rate at matched load alongside.

## Lanes
  overlap-O1  stage-idle       (F1 side A) + S1 S2 S4
  overlap-O2  cache-budgeted   (F1 side B) + S1 S2 S4
  reorder-R1  head-promotion   (F2 side A) + S1 S2 S3 S4
  reorder-R2  cost-class       (F2 side B) + S1 S2 S3 S4
Four lanes, not seven. Each gets this file, HISTORY-overlap-reorder.md, and the judging rules.
Lanes code freely; the box is scheduled by mainline, one measuring lane at a time.

# Cache competition (owner addition 2026-09-13)

## What already exists -- do not rediscover it
The cache-utilisation audit (cx-cacheutil, CACHEUTIL.md, 2026-09-10) got as far as a ranked
candidate list with predictions recorded BEFORE measurement, IBS demand-miss attribution across all
12 workers, a source-derived hot/cold field map for Op/Client/ROB/ThreadCtx/Shard/FlatStore, and one
isolated PRE/POST: candidate 1 (move the every-command `total_commands_` store off the ThreadCtx
line that peers read) measured cycles/op -3.36% on 1s GET p32, IPC +3.9%, instr/op +0.4% -- triage
grade (box was shared). It never reached a verdict because its measurement window kept being
contended. That table is the starting point; the audit's own words: "these are sampled-demand
rankings, not an additive allocation of all fills/op". Two recorded laws govern this work:
  * COHERENCE NOT-HIDING: load stalls hide behind other work at saturation; producer STORES into
    lines a consumer reads (RFO) do not. Rank candidates by RFOs removed, not misses removed.
  * LAYOUT SENSITIVITY: pure code placement moves a 2s GET cell +-0.7%; a sub-1% claim needs a
    padding control. Layout locks (Op 336, Client 1984, ThreadCtx 1408, Shard 1440, FlatStore 944,
    Rob<64> 192, AtomicEntry 144) must hold or be re-locked with a stated reason.

## Structure: one fork, shared mechanisms, same judging

### Fork
  F3  WHERE THE CACHE IS LOST: layout (L1) vs access pattern (L2).
      L1 says the hot structures are laid out badly -- hot and cold fields share lines, an every-op
      store sits on a peer-read line, Op/Client headers straddle -- and the fix is packing: the
      audit's candidates 1, 2, 3 and 5, taken as far as the layout locks allow, each measured
      alone (C3) and ranked by RFOs removed. L2 says layout is secondary and the loss is in WHICH
      lines a stage touches and WHEN -- so the fix is access ordering: touch a structure's lines in
      one pass per stage, hoist the per-op reads of ThreadCtx/Shard out of the per-op loop into
      per-batch locals, and prefetch to a measured window (this is where it meets overlap O2). They
      disagree about whether fills/op falls more from moving fields or from moving code. Both must
      report fills/op AND RFOs/op AND cycles/op; the fork is decided on cycles/op with the others
      as explanation.

### Shared mechanisms (both lanes)
  S5  RFO ranking. Every candidate is ranked by producer-stores-into-consumer-lines removed, from
      IBS, before any is built. A candidate that removes only load misses is deprioritised: at
      saturation those hide.
  S6  Padding control. Every layout or placement change ships with a pad-only twin -- same size
      change, no field moved -- so a +-0.7% placement artefact cannot be reported as a win.
  S7  Locks stay locked. sizeof static_asserts hold; a change that needs a lock moved states the
      new size and why, and the gate's footprint row must agree.
  S4  Amortization per mechanism, as above -- for cache work the "fixed cost" is footprint growth
      and the "per-op cost" is any added indirection; a sidecar that saves a line but adds a
      pointer chase must show the chase is cheaper than the line.

### Constraints: C1-C4 apply unchanged. The cell that most often flips sign on cache changes is 2s
GET p32 (recorded), so it is mandatory in both arms.

### Lanes
  cache-L1  layout    (F3 side A) + S4 S5 S6 S7
  cache-L2  access    (F3 side B) + S4 S5 S6 S7
Both start from the audit's candidate table and IBS data in cx-cacheutil/, not from scratch. Both
must first REPRODUCE candidate 1's -3.36% on a quiet box at confirmation grade -- if it does not
reproduce, the audit's attribution is suspect and both lanes say so before building anything else.

## Interaction with overlap
O2 (cache-budgeted overlap) and L2 (access ordering) share a mechanism -- prefetch to a measured
window. They are built in different lanes on purpose: O2 asks whether overlap's p32 ceiling is
residency; L2 asks whether the steady-state working set is touched efficiently. If both win, the
merge is one mechanism, not two; if one wins and the other loses, that tells us which question was
the real one. Mainline reconciles at merge time; the lanes do not coordinate.

## All six lanes
  overlap-O1  overlap-O2  reorder-R1  reorder-R2  cache-L1  cache-L2
Six codex lanes, six worktrees, coding in parallel; the box is scheduled one measuring lane at a
time by mainline. Merge order after judging: cache first (it changes the floor the other two are
measured against), then overlap, then reorder, then coadapt.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Same-session headline ABBA gate. No historical rate is a performance target.

WHY NOT STORED REFERENCE NUMBERS. A stored rate goes stale the moment the kernel, compiler,
microcode or machine changes; this tree's old tests/gate_refs.txt was pinned to a kernel that no
longer runs, and the gate's own comments then called every verdict provisional. Measuring both arms
in ONE session on ONE box removes drift, thermal state and machine configuration as variables. The
only difference left between the arms is the code.

THE REFERENCE is the caller's --reference-binary, whose digest is recorded and matched against a
last-push manifest pin when available. Without that argument, origin/cpp is resolved to a full
commit id, then matched against /home/user/Projects/bench-bins/MANIFEST.md. A filename containing
"headline" is NOT evidence of identity; two different digests for one commit are ambiguous and skip.
Missing or unbuildable reference => loud SKIP, never a pass: a correctness-only run must not be able
to call itself a clean gate.

ABBA, NOT A-THEN-B. Every cell runs reference, candidate, candidate, reference and takes the paired
difference. Non-interleaved A/B has produced wrong verdicts on this box before, and a 20-second
window exposes drift that a 90-second window hides. ABBA cancels a LINEAR trend when the run
midpoints are evenly spaced; it cannot promise cancellation of arbitrary interference, periodic
noise or nonlinear drift, so both arm spreads are always reported and a quiet box still matters.

THE THRESHOLD IS DERIVED, NOT CHOSEN. T for a block IS that block's observed reference spread
(100*|A2-A1|/Abar). There is no 3% default, no fixed noise floor, no multiplier, no historical
calibration, and no candidate-dependent widening. A quiet box therefore produces a STRICTER gate,
which is the correct incentive. Two samples measure an observed span, not a confidence interval:
the gate detects losses larger than that span, and a loss inside it is below the session's own
demonstrated resolution -- say that, do not pretend to more.

THE 2% INSTABILITY BOUNDARY IS A VALIDITY CHECK, NOT A REGRESSION ALLOWANCE. An arm whose spread
exceeds 2% fails the MEASUREMENT. Without this, a wildly noisy reference manufactures a permissive
threshold and waves a real regression through. A failed block is never rerun until it happens to
pass, and the best of several runs is never selected.

SATURATION IS A PRECONDITION, not a nice-to-have: an unsaturated cell has headroom that absorbs a
regression, so it cannot detect one at any repetition count. Pinned load levels run one ABBA block
and must still satisfy the productive-role occupancy floor. Unpinned cells, or --escalate,
search until EACH arm stops gaining AND its productive bottleneck role meets the floor.
Raw legacy all-thread busy is retained but cannot penalize legitimate idle executors.
Depth 1 is exempt and
scored as latency -- it is round-trip bound by Little's law. Process CPU is NOT substituted for busy
percentage: doing so hides exactly the unsaturated case this check exists to catch.

THE VERDICT NAMES THE WORST CELL. It is the conjunction of cell verdicts; no average across GET,
SET, thread modes or cells can hide the one cell that fails. A failed precondition outranks passing
cells. --only is a diagnostic selection and yields PARTIAL with exit 3, never a complete-tier pass.

Exit 0: every cell passed; 1: failure; 3: loud skip or successful partial diagnostic.
Comparison PASS additionally requires a recent matching standing null. Missing/invalid controls
leave successful measurements PARTIAL and untrusted. --collect-null 1 freezes identical arms and
collects its own null verdict without a prior control; its outer PARTIAL/3 cannot gate a push.
--self-test is serverless. All other runs own and reap only their subprocess PIDs.
"""

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
WINDOW = 20
WARMUP = 3
TAIL = 5
KEYS = 2_000_000
MIN_BUSY = 98.0        # the busy level we PREFER, and still record; no longer a hard gate
BUSY_FLOOR = SATURATION_FLOOR  # productive-role occupancy; plateau remains independently required
# Run-to-run scatter of one binary's own rate and occupancy on identical bytes, measured by the
# standing nulls (0.71%; 0.6-1.0% across 15 cells). Used to decide when two saturated rungs are the
# same plateau, and how far a single occupancy sample may sit under the floor before the block is
# judged unsaturated. Lives here because load_calibration imports this module.
PLATEAU_TOLERANCE_PCT = 1.0
# Read-local cells above depth 1 run at this box's highest throughput (54-56 Mops/s on GET p32) and
# repeat far less tightly than the rest: measured on IDENTICAL bytes, h11 4.56%, h31 4.62%,
# h27 5.44%, h15 6.51%, against 0.08-1.8% for every non-read-local cell in the same run. Their
# threshold floors here so the tier stops reporting its own scatter as a regression. The cost is
# stated plainly: a real read-local regression smaller than this is not detectable by this cell,
# and needs the multi-instance variance explained rather than a tighter number.
READ_LOCAL_THRESHOLD_FLOOR_PCT = 5.0


def saturation_exempt(cell):
    """Cells whose verdict is a LATENCY, so an occupancy floor does not protect it.

    The floor exists so a throughput regression cannot hide in server headroom. A tail-latency
    verdict is not protected by it: p99.9 does not improve because the server is busier. Depth 1
    was already exempt for this reason; the blocker-mix reorder cells need the same treatment and
    for a stronger reason -- their workload DELIBERATELY idles the server on long commands, so they
    sit at or under the floor by construction. Measured 2026-09-12 on identical bytes: t03 ran
    92.0-96.4% occupancy across six rungs and could never pin, t01 95.4/95.5, t02 96.7/97.4,
    t04 93.7-97.9. Requiring 95% of them asks the workload not to be what it is.
    """
    return cell.depth == 1 or cell.metric == "p999_ms"
#
# SATURATION IS ESTABLISHED BY A RATE PLATEAU, NOT BY A BUSY PERCENTAGE ALONE (owner ruling
# 2026-09-10). Demanding >=98% busy in every run fails a candidate FOR BEING FASTER: a quicker
# server does the same offered work with less CPU, so on 2026-09-10 the h12 SET cell sat at 97.1%
# busy while delivering 24.6 Mops/s against the reference's 22.2 at 98.4% -- an 11% gain the gate
# refused to certify. Adding 50% more load generator threads did not move it; the server simply
# could not be pinned at 98% by any load this box can offer.
#
# Escalation judges the lowest TESTED saturated rung whose two arms stop gaining beyond
# their own measured repeatability under a stable, higher-worker-capacity probe. A stable
# decline may confirm the earlier saturated rung but is explicitly labeled congestion:
# h12 peaked at 26.6 Mops/s with 2 instances and decayed to 24.6 by 16. Neither that decline
# nor a worker-count increase proves unused generator headroom. Never pad a pin into it.
# Load-generator escalation ladder. 8 was not enough: on 2026-09-10 the h12 SET cell left the
# CANDIDATE arm at 97.1% busy while the reference sat at 98.4%, because the candidate was 10.7%
# faster and therefore did the same offered work with less CPU. A faster server needs MORE load to
# saturate, so capping the ladder at 8 makes an improvement fail the saturation precondition -- the
# gate would reject exactly the changes it exists to certify. The preferred diagnostic
# level remains 98%; the enforced BUSY_FLOOR above is unchanged.
# At 512 connections on the default 192 load CPUs, n=12 assigns 16 workers per
# process and two or three clients per worker: all 192 workers serve exactly 512
# connections. n=8 uses 128 workers; n=16 also uses only 128 because its equal
# connection shares must divide the worker count. Keep n=16 as a separate probe,
# but selection must not credit its smaller worker pool as increased capacity.
LADDER = (1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16)
# Project measurement-integrity boundary, NOT the regression tolerance.
MAX_SPREAD = 2.0
ORDER = ("A", "B", "B", "A")


class Skip(RuntimeError):
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Cell:
    id: str
    mode: str
    read_local: int
    overlap: int
    reorder: int
    op: str
    depth: int
    conns: int
    instances: int = 0     # PINNED load-generator instance count; 0 = unpinned, search for it
    atomic: int = 1
    score: str = "auto"
    mix: str = "-"         # READ:WRITE for MIX/MIX8; short:long for REORDER
    smoke: bool = False
    pin_required: bool = False

    @property
    def metric(self):
        return ("latency_ms" if self.depth == 1 else "rate") if self.score == "auto" else {
            "rate": "rate", "latency": "latency_ms", "p999": "p999_ms"}[self.score]


def read_cells(path, *, placement=None):
    cells = []
    measurements = load_measurements()
    instrument = (instrument_digest() if any(floor["status"] == "calibrated"
                  for floor in measurements["load_floors"].values()) else None)
    for lineno, line in enumerate(path.read_text().splitlines(), 1):
        if not line.strip() or line.lstrip().startswith("#"):
            continue
        fields = [x.strip() for x in line.split("|")]
        if len(fields) not in (11, 15):
            raise ValueError(f"{path}:{lineno}: expected 11 legacy or 15 extended pipe-separated fields")
        ident, mode, rl, ov, ro, op, depth, conns, _measured, _busy, pinned = fields[:11]
        if (not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_-]+", ident) or mode not in ("1s", "2s")
                or op not in ("GET", "SET", "MGET", "MSET", "MIX", "MIX8", "REORDER")
                or not re.fullmatch(r"p[1-9][0-9]*", depth)
                or not re.fullmatch(r"[1-9][0-9]*", conns)
                or any(not re.fullmatch(prefix + "=[01]", value)
                       for prefix, value in (("rl", rl), ("ov", ov), ("ro", ro)))):
            raise ValueError(f"{path}:{lineno}: unsupported/malformed cell: {line}")
        # Production measurements have one home. The reserved legacy columns remain
        # readable for private diagnostic fixtures, whose pins never modify production.
        if path.resolve() == (ROOT / "tests/headline_cells.txt").resolve() and fields[8:11] != ["-"] * 3:
            raise ValueError(f"{path}:{lineno}: measurements belong in gate_measurements.json")
        extra = {}
        if len(fields) == 15:
            atomic, score, mix, smoke = fields[11:]
            if (not re.fullmatch(r"atomic=[01]", atomic)
                    or score not in ("score=rate", "score=latency", "score=p999")
                    or not re.fullmatch(r"mix=(-|[1-9][0-9]*:[1-9][0-9]*)", mix)
                    or not re.fullmatch(r"smoke=[01]", smoke)
                    or not re.fullmatch(r"-|[1-9][0-9]*", pinned)):
                raise ValueError(f"{path}:{lineno}: malformed extended workload fields")
            extra = dict(atomic=int(atomic[-1]), score=score[6:], mix=mix[4:],
                         smoke=smoke[-1] == "1", pin_required=int(depth[1:]) > 1)
        cell = Cell(ident, mode, int(rl[-1]), int(ov[-1]), int(ro[-1]),
                    op, int(depth[1:]), int(conns),
                    int(pinned) if re.fullmatch(r"[1-9][0-9]*", pinned) else 0, **extra)
        if ((cell.op in ("MIX", "MIX8", "REORDER")) != (cell.mix != "-")
                or (cell.op == "REORDER") != (cell.metric == "p999_ms")
                or (cell.depth == 1 and cell.metric == "rate")):
            raise ValueError(f"{path}:{lineno}: workload, mix and scoring disagree")
        if pinned == "-":
            cell = apply_floor(cell, measurements, placement=placement, instrument_sha256=instrument)
        cells.append(cell)
    if not cells or len({c.id for c in cells}) != len(cells):
        raise ValueError("headline cells must be nonempty with unique IDs")
    return cells


def selected_cells(cells, subset, only=""):
    selected = [cell for cell in cells if subset == "full" or cell.smoke]
    if not selected:
        raise ValueError(f"cell source has no {subset} cells")
    if only:
        requested = set(only.split(","))
        if requested - {cell.id for cell in selected}:
            raise ValueError("--only names a cell absent from the selected subset")
        selected = [cell for cell in selected if cell.id in requested]
    return selected


def coverage(cells):
    return {"count": len(cells), "ids": [cell.id for cell in cells],
            "modes": sorted({cell.mode for cell in cells}),

CXX      ?= g++
JEDIR    ?= /home/user/Projects/refs/jemalloc/_install
# jemalloc is optional: without it the tree still builds and runs, using the deterministic portable
# size-class table in alloc.h. Set JE=0 to force that path (useful for A/B-ing the allocator).
JE       ?= 1
ifeq ($(JE),1)
  # Prefer the system package; fall back to the copy built from refs/.
  ifneq ($(wildcard /usr/include/jemalloc/jemalloc.h),)
    JEFLAGS := -DTOMO_JEMALLOC
    JELIBS  := -ljemalloc
  else
    JEFLAGS := -DTOMO_JEMALLOC -I$(JEDIR)/include
    JELIBS  := $(JEDIR)/lib/libjemalloc.a -ldl
  endif
else
  JEFLAGS :=
  JELIBS  :=
endif
CXXFLAGS ?= -std=c++20 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -march=native -pthread
LDLIBS   ?= -luring -pthread
SRC      := src/main.cc src/net/tls.cc src/cmd/commands.cc src/cmd/glob.cc src/cmd/xshard.cc src/cmd/acl.cc src/cmd/hll.cc src/cmd/t_server.cc src/cmd/t_string.cc src/cmd/t_string_notify.cc src/cmd/t_hash.cc src/cmd/t_hash_ttl.cc \
            src/cmd/t_list.cc src/cmd/t_set.cc src/cmd/t_zset.cc src/cmd/t_zset_ops.cc src/cmd/geo.cc src/cmd/t_stream.cc src/cmd/t_stream_groups.cc src/cmd/scripting.cc src/cmd/functions.cc src/cmd/serialize.cc src/snapshot/snapshot.cc src/persist/aof.cc
SRC      += src/cmd/climon.cc src/cmd/tracking.cc
SRC      += src/cmd/server_tail.cc src/cmd/slowlog.cc src/cmd/lcs.cc src/cmd/info_stats.cc
SRC      += src/cmd/lbsignals.cc
SRC      += src/core/flipctl.cc
SRC      += src/core/genthread.cc
SRC      += src/core/rl2s.cc
SRC      += src/cmd/cmdgap.cc
SRC      += src/cmd/pfdebug.cc
SRC      += src/cmd/cmdmeta.cc
SRC      += src/cmd/t_sort.cc
LDLIBS   += -lssl -lcrypto
BIN      := build/tomokv
OBJ      := $(SRC:%.cc=build/%.o)

all: $(BIN)

$(BIN): $(OBJ)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(OBJ) -o $@ $(JELIBS) $(LDLIBS) -lm

# The clean string family intentionally excludes the armed instantiations, but its parsed template
# bodies still move GCC just past the default large-unit threshold. 10600 restores the same inlining
# decisions as the base-420b4d492 translation unit; the objdump gate locks cmd_get/cmd_set to base.
build/src/cmd/t_string.o: CXXFLAGS += --param large-unit-insns=10600

build/%.o: %.cc $(wildcard src/*/*.h) $(wildcard src/*/*.inc) $(wildcard third_party/lua/*) Makefile
	@mkdir -p $(dir $@)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(JEFLAGS) -I. -c $< -o $@

asan: CXXFLAGS += -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -O1
asan:
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. $(SRC) -o build/tomokv-asan $(LDLIBS) -lm

tsan:
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) -std=c++20 -O1 -g -Wall -Wextra -pthread -fsanitize=thread \
	  -I. $(SRC) -o build/tomokv-tsan $(LDLIBS) -lm

# The armed-write block cache's ownership laws as assertions: the cache and the QSBR retire ring
# are owner-private (one thread, no lock), each cached block is resident exactly once, each class
# list matches its counter, and every shard's retire sink names its CURRENT owner. Debug-only: the
# residency set and the sampled list walk cost far more than the path they guard. DESIGN-P0REPLY.md.
rlcachedbg:
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(JEFLAGS) -DTOMO_RL_CACHE_DEBUG -I. $(SRC) \
	  -o build/tomokv-rlcachedbg $(JELIBS) $(LDLIBS) -lm

# NEGATIVE-CONTROL BUILD for the row above: the same assertions with the ownership-edge rebind
# removed, i.e. the pre-fix behaviour. tests/rlcache_churn.py MUST fail against this binary; a
# detector that cannot report failure proves nothing about the runs that pass.
rlcache-nofix:
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(JEFLAGS) -DTOMO_RL_CACHE_DEBUG -DTOMO_RL_CACHE_NO_EAGER_ADOPT -I. $(SRC) \
	  -o build/tomokv-rlcache-nofix $(JELIBS) $(LDLIBS) -lm

# NEGATIVE-CONTROL BUILD for the cross-owner script reservation sub-wave. Identical to the release
# build except that ScriptPhase::Pin arms nothing, so tests/xscript.py counterexample MUST fail
# against it. A detector that cannot report failure proves nothing about the runs that pass.
noreserve:
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(JEFLAGS) -DTOMO_XSCRIPT_NO_RESERVE -I. $(SRC) \
	  -o build/tomokv-noreserve $(JELIBS) $(LDLIBS) -lm

# Server-less unit binaries: the config parser and the flip controller. `make unit` builds and
# runs both (neither boots a server). tests/gate.sh's parser row is the same program.
build/config-parser-test: tests/config_parser_test.cc $(wildcard src/*/*.h) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. tests/config_parser_test.cc -o $@
build/flipctl-unit: tests/flipctl_unit.cc src/core/flipctl.cc $(wildcard src/*/*.h) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. tests/flipctl_unit.cc src/core/flipctl.cc -o $@
# The fused owner's deferred-reclaim ring (QSBR batches) against a per-entry reference model.
build/read-local-ring-unit: tests/read_local_ring_unit.cc $(wildcard src/*/*.h) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. tests/read_local_ring_unit.cc -o $@
build/read-local-write-ring-unit: tests/read_local_write_ring_unit.cc $(wildcard src/*/*.h) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. tests/read_local_write_ring_unit.cc -o $@
# The production cross-connection scheduler, with real ROB tasks at both executor capacities.
build/reorder-unit: tests/reorder_unit.cc $(wildcard src/*/*.h) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. tests/reorder_unit.cc -o $@
STORE_REGRESSION_SRC := tests/store_regression.cc src/cmd/t_hash.cc src/cmd/t_hash_ttl.cc
build/store-regression: $(STORE_REGRESSION_SRC) $(wildcard src/*/*.h) $(wildcard src/*/*.inc) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -DTOMO_STORE_REGRESSION_TEST -I. \
	  $(STORE_REGRESSION_SRC) -Wl,--gc-sections -o $@
build/store-regression-sidecar: $(STORE_REGRESSION_SRC) $(wildcard src/*/*.h) $(wildcard src/*/*.inc) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -DTOMO_STORE_REGRESSION_TEST \
	  -DTOMO_TTL_DEADLINE_SIDECAR=1 -I. $(STORE_REGRESSION_SRC) -Wl,--gc-sections -o $@
build/store-regression-tsan: $(STORE_REGRESSION_SRC) $(wildcard src/*/*.h) $(wildcard src/*/*.inc) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -O1 -fsanitize=thread -fno-omit-frame-pointer -no-pie \
	  -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -DTOMO_STORE_REGRESSION_TEST -I. \
	  $(STORE_REGRESSION_SRC) -Wl,--gc-sections -o $@
build/waits-unit: tests/waits_unit.cc $(wildcard src/*/*.h) Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. tests/waits_unit.cc -o $@
unit: build/config-parser-test build/flipctl-unit build/read-local-ring-unit build/read-local-write-ring-unit build/reorder-unit build/waits-unit
	./build/config-parser-test
	./build/flipctl-unit
	./build/read-local-ring-unit
	./build/read-local-write-ring-unit
	./build/reorder-unit
	./build/waits-unit

# Deterministic core regressions: the test TU instantiates the real executor/IO methods
# with ASAN/UBSAN and test-only interleaving hooks. No server or ring is started.
CORE_TEST_OBJ := $(filter-out build/src/main.o build/src/core/genthread.o,$(OBJ))
build/rehash-waits-unit: tests/rehash_waits_unit.cc $(CORE_TEST_OBJ) $(wildcard src/*/*.h) Makefile
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(JEFLAGS) -I. $< $(CORE_TEST_OBJ) -o $@ $(JELIBS) $(LDLIBS) -lm

build/core-concurrency-unit: tests/core_concurrency_unit.cc $(CORE_TEST_OBJ) $(wildcard src/*/*.h)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(JEFLAGS) -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer \
	  -DTOMO_CORE_CONCURRENCY_TEST -I. $< $(CORE_TEST_OBJ) -o $@ \
	  $(JELIBS) $(LDLIBS) -lm

# Directed owner-phase tests. The test includes xshard.cc to drive the real private phases
# without starting worker threads or opening a listener; all other code is the release objects.
build/atomic-survivors-unit: tests/atomic_survivors_unit.cc src/cmd/xshard.cc $(filter-out build/src/main.o build/src/cmd/xshard.o,$(OBJ)) $(wildcard src/*/*.inc) $(wildcard src/*/*.h) Makefile
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(JEFLAGS) -I. tests/atomic_survivors_unit.cc \
	  $(filter-out build/src/main.o build/src/cmd/xshard.o,$(OBJ)) -o $@ $(JELIBS) $(LDLIBS) -lm

# Load drivers: not part of `all`, kept compiling here so they cannot rot unnoticed.
build/benchtxn: tools/benchtxn.cc Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. tools/benchtxn.cc -o $@
build/broaden-bench: tests/broaden_bench.cc Makefile
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -I. tests/broaden_bench.cc -o $@
tools: build/benchtxn build/broaden-bench

clean:
	rm -rf build
.PHONY: all asan tsan noreserve clean unit tools

# Deterministic networking/command regressions. These TUs include the real private implementations;
# omit their production objects from this serverless binary. No server threads or gate are started.
NETCMD_TEST_SRC := tests/netcmd_unit.cc tests/netcmd_stream_unit.cc tests/netcmd_zset_unit.cc tests/netcmd_config_unit.cc
NETCMD_TEST_OBJ := $(NETCMD_TEST_SRC:tests/%.cc=build/tests/%.o)
NETCMD_LIB_OBJ := $(filter-out build/src/main.o build/src/cmd/xshard.o build/src/cmd/t_stream_groups.o build/src/cmd/t_zset.o build/src/cmd/server_tail.o,$(OBJ))
build/tests/%.o: tests/%.cc tests/netcmd_unit.h $(wildcard src/*/*.h) $(wildcard src/*/*.cc) $(wildcard src/*/*.inc) Makefile
	@mkdir -p $(dir $@)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(JEFLAGS) -Wno-mismatched-new-delete -I. -c $< -o $@
build/netcmd-unit: $(NETCMD_TEST_OBJ) $(NETCMD_LIB_OBJ)

# TomoKV — project context for codex

Prepend this to every codex prompt. It is the shared background; each prompt then states its own scope.
Written 2026-09-07. Baseline commit `78c3e5391` (`origin/cpp`), full gate 344/344.

## What it is

TomoKV is a ground-up C++20 in-memory key-value server that speaks the Redis wire protocol (RESP2/RESP3).
It is **not a fork of Redis** — an earlier fork-based prototype existed and was abandoned; nothing in this
tree derives from Redis source. It implements **243 registered commands**. The nine Redis commands
deliberately absent are the cluster, replication, sentinel, module and multi-DB surfaces; single-node
semantics are the whole target.

It is a research system. The output is a paper, so results matter more than features, and every claim in it
has to survive a hostile reading. Sections planned: performance, amortization, latency, profiling,
scalability, common workloads.

## Architecture

**Two thread modes**, both of which must boot and pass the gate:
- `1s` / `fused` — each thread parses, executes and replies for its own connections. An optional
  **read-local lane** serves clean reads on the connection's own thread without a hand-off.
- `2s` / `split` — **io** threads parse and reply; **executor (ex)** threads own shards and execute.
  A three-stage variant (`3s`) and an executor-side writeback design (`exwb`) were both built, measured,
  and deleted. Do not propose either.

**Sharding and ownership.** Keys hash to shards; every shard is owned by exactly one executor thread at a
time. Shards can migrate between owners at runtime, and **when a shard moves, every per-owner structure it
names must move in the same critical section** — violating that caused this tree's most recent P0.

**Ordering ring (`rob`).** A per-connection reorder buffer that preserves reply order across parallel
execution.

**Atomics.** Multi-key atomicity uses group-scoped epoch-MVCC. Cross-shard commands use scatter-gather.
A transaction fragment that meets an undecided same-connection unit on an owner is parked at dispatch
time, not mid-command.

**Flip.** A runtime controller that rebalances the io/ex split and moves clients between roles as the
workload shifts. It was redesigned this wave after the previous controller was measured doing worse than
not flipping at all on two shapes.

**Load balancing.** Key-affine and client-affine balancing (`--key-lb`, `--client-lb`), both default on.

Networking is io_uring; the allocator is jemalloc.

## Non-negotiable correctness laws

Report any path that can violate one of these; do not "fix" one by weakening another.
- Single-owner writes.
- Reads are never obstructed by writes: immutable replacement plus QSBR. **No reader retries and no
  seqlocks on the per-operation path.**
- In-place overwrite is banned while the read-local lane is armed.
- Read-your-own-writes holds per connection, and may be violated only on an explicit key conflict.
- Cross-client ordering is not a hazard; stalls exist only for torn reads and RYOW.
- Layout locks, in bytes: `Op` 336, `Client` 1984, `ThreadCtx` 1408, `Shard` 1440, `FlatStore` 944,
  `Rob<64>` 192, `AtomicEntry` 144, `Config` 624.
- Both thread modes boot. Main commands carry zero regression. One file per feature.

## The box

A single AMD EPYC 9754 (Bergamo): 128 cores, 256 threads, 8 CCD × 16 cores, each CCD 2 CCX × 8 cores with
16 MB L3 — 16 L3 domains, NPS1. Measured node optimum is 8 cores, one CCX. Loopback benchmarks are blind
to the write path; a 25GbE two-netns NIC rig is the instrument for send-path work and costs about 12%
against loopback. Box noise is ±0.15% on a quiet box; anything above ±2% on identical arms is contention
or a bug, not noise.

**The gate boots nothing like a default server.** `tests/gate.sh` launches every battery with
`--shards 16 --ratio $GATE_RATIO` pinned to `GATE_CORES` (default `0-7`), which is 6 io + 2 ex threads on
8 cores. Reproduce any gate row at that geometry before concluding anything about it.

## What it is measured against

Redis 7.4 and 8.8.1, Dragonfly 1.40.2, KeyDB, Microsoft Garnet (net10.0), memcached 1.6.45, plus YCSB
0.17.0 traces. Binaries and digests: `/home/user/Projects/bench-bins/MANIFEST.md`.

We do not win everywhere and the paper will not claim we do. At 64 real cores and pipeline depth 128,
Garnet reaches 62.8M ops/s against our 34.4M. We hold depth 1, where we reach 4.35M. Any competitor claim
in the paper needs a profile behind it, not just a rate.

## How performance is judged

**cycles/op = instructions/op ÷ IPC.** Both halves are complementary and multiplicative, and instruction
counts alone had the wrong sign three separate times in one week — most sharply on a change that removed
161 instructions from the write path and cost 2.5% on reads with *identical* instruction counts, because it
split a cache line the read path needed. Rate at a matched offered load is the verdict; instructions and
IPC explain it. Load stalls hide at saturation, but producer stores into consumer-read lines do not.

Every optimization lands with a PRE vs POST table. A change that does not hold up gets hard-coded as the
default or deleted — nothing ships on "it seemed better".

## Why this work looks the way it does

Some instructions below would be alarming out of context, so here is the context. This is a single-user
research box. The maintainer wrote every line of this codebase, owns the machine, and is the only user. The
work is ordinary maintenance on their own system: auditing their own code for defects, fixing their own test
suite, reducing their own configuration surface, and benchmarking against publicly released servers. Nothing
here touches anyone else's data, systems or accounts.

Four specifics that read oddly without the reason:

1. **"Never run the server, the benchmark or the gate."** This is about measurement integrity and nothing
   else. Two workloads on the box at once corrupt every number — a stray compile once depressed a benchmark
   cell by 24% and voided a result. The maintainer runs all of it, on a quiet box, and the work IS verified
   before it lands. You are being asked to produce a diff, not to skip verification.

2. **"Never edit `EXPECT_QUICK` / `EXPECT_FULL`."** Those constants are how many test rows must pass. Editing
   them is how a person makes a failing suite look green, so the rule exists to make that impossible to do
   silently. It is a stricter standard than normal, not a looser one. State what the count should become and
   why; the maintainer changes it.

3. **Concurrency vocabulary.** This is a database. "Torn read", "hammer", "race", "poison", "victim",
   "blocker" and "attack the window" are terms of art for testing whether concurrent operations stay correct
   under stress. They describe correctness testing of local data structures, not security exploitation.

4. **Deliberately breaking a mechanism to check a test.** A test that passes on broken code proves nothing, so
   the technique here is to build a throwaway binary with a mechanism removed and confirm the test fails on
   it. That build is never committed and never runs outside the box. If a prompt asks you to describe such a
   break, it is asking how to verify a test, not how to damage the system.

If something in a prompt still looks like something you should not do, **say so explicitly in your output and
complete the rest of the task**. A stated objection is useful. Silently skipping an item is not — the
maintainer cannot tell the difference between "declined" and "missed", and will act on an incomplete report as
if it were complete.

## Working rules for codex

- **Never run a server, a benchmark, or the gate.** The maintainer runs the box. Report, or produce a diff.
- Edit only inside your own worktree.
- Never edit `EXPECT_QUICK` / `EXPECT_FULL` in `tests/gate.sh`. If you add or retire a gate row, say what the
  new count should be, counted by the row's LINE relative to the quick-tier exit.
- Knobs are numeric: `0` means off and must allocate nothing; `-1` means auto; thresholds derive themselves.
  Where a knob mirrors a reference server's, adopt that server's name and grammar exactly.
- A test that cannot fail proves nothing. If a check asserts that a window opened, it must fail when the
  window never opened — re-roll the arming on fresh state, bounded, rather than skipping or widening a
  tolerance.

## Closed doors — measured, negative, do not re-propose

`3s` three-stage mode; `exwb` executor-side writeback (−11 to −22%); AMAC and any CR/MR split (the only
boundary is io/ex); reorder-and-window; seqlocks on the per-op path; connection-side record allocation
(`connalloc`, cycles flat, record born on the wrong core); executor-major task collapse (`exmajor`,
−2 to −3%); the read-local capacity hand-off line split (`t-pubdiet`, +1.97% SET but −2.50% GET).

It is the shared background; each prompt then states its own scope. Written 2026-09-07. Baseline commit `78c3e5391` (`origin/cpp`), full gate 344/344.  ## What it is  TomoKV is a ground-up C++20 in-memory key-value server that speaks the Redis wire protocol (RESP2/RESP3). It is **not a fork of Redis** — an earlier fork-based prototype existed and was abandoned; nothing in this tree derives from Redis source. It implements **243 registered commands**. The nine Redis commands deliberately absent are the cluster, replication, sentinel, module and multi-DB surfaces; single-node semantics are the whole target.  It is a research system. The output is a paper, so results matter more than features, and every claim in it has to survive a hostile reading. Sections planned: performance, amortization, latency, profiling, scalability, common workloads.  ## Architecture  **Two thread modes**, both of which must boot and pass the gate: - `1s` / `fused` — each thread parses, executes and replies for its own connections. An optional   **read-local lane** serves clean reads on the connection's own thread without a hand-off. - `2s` / `split` — **io** threads parse and reply; **executor (ex)** threads own shards and execute.   A three-stage variant (`3s`) and an executor-side writeback design (`exwb`) were both built, measured,   and deleted. Do not propose either.  **Sharding and ownership.** Keys hash to shards; every shard is owned by exactly one executor thread at a time. Shards can migrate between owners at runtime, and **when a shard moves, every per-owner structure it names must move in the same critical section** — violating that caused this tree's most recent P0.  **Ordering ring (`rob`).** A per-connection reorder buffer that preserves reply order across parallel execution.  **Atomics.** Multi-key atomicity uses group-scoped epoch-MVCC. Cross-shard commands use scatter-gather. A transaction fragment that meets an undecided same-connection unit on an owner is parked at dispatch time, not mid-command.  **Flip.** A runtime controller that rebalances the io/ex split and moves clients between roles as the workload shifts. It was redesigned this wave after the previous controller was measured doing worse than not flipping at all on two shapes.  **Load balancing.** Key-affine and client-affine balancing (`--key-lb`, `--client-lb`), both default on.  Networking is io_uring; the allocator is jemalloc.  ## Non-negotiable correctness laws  Report any path that can violate one of these; do not "fix" one by weakening another. - Single-owner writes. - Reads are never obstructed by writes: immutable replacement plus QSBR. **No reader retries and no   seqlocks on the per-operation path.** - In-place overwrite is banned while the read-local lane is armed. - Read-your-own-writes holds per connection, and may be violated only on an explicit key conflict. - Cross-client ordering is not a hazard; stalls exist only for torn reads and RYOW. - Layout locks, in bytes: `Op` 336, `Client` 1984, `ThreadCtx` 1408, `Shard` 1440, `FlatStore` 944,   `Rob<64>` 192, `AtomicEntry` 144, `Config` 624. - Both thread modes boot. Main commands carry zero regression. One file per feature.  ## The box  A single AMD EPYC 9754 (Bergamo): 128 cores, 256 threads, 8 CCD × 16 cores, each CCD 2 CCX × 8 cores with 16 MB L3 — 16 L3 domains, NPS1. Measured node optimum is 8 cores, one CCX. Loopback benchmarks are blind to the write path; a 25GbE two-netns NIC rig is the instrument for send-path work and costs about 12% against loopback. Box noise is ±0.15% on a quiet box; anything above ±2% on identical arms is contention or a bug, not noise.  **The gate boots nothing like a default server.** `tests/gate.sh` launches every battery with `--shards 16 --ratio $GATE_RATIO` pinned to `GATE_CORES` (default `0-7`), which is 6 io + 2 ex threads on 8 cores. Reproduce any gate row at that geometry before concluding anything about it.  ## What it is measured against  Redis 7.4 and 8.8.1, Dragonfly 1.40.2, KeyDB, Microsoft Garnet (net10.0), memcached 1.6.45, plus YCSB 0.17.0 traces. Binaries and digests: `/home/user/Projects/bench-bins/MANIFEST.md`.  We do not win everywhere and the paper will not claim we do. At 64 real cores and pipeline depth 128, Garnet reaches 62.8M ops/s against our 34.4M. We hold depth 1, where we reach 4.35M. Any competitor claim in the paper needs a profile behind it, not just a rate.  ## How performance is judged  **cycles/op = instructions/op ÷ IPC.** Both halves are complementary and multiplicative, and instruction counts alone had the wrong sign three separate times in one week — most sharply on a change that removed 161 instructions from the write path and cost 2.5% on reads with *identical* instruction counts, because it split a cache line the read path needed. Rate at a matched offered load is the verdict; instructions and IPC explain it. Load stalls hide at saturation, but producer stores into consumer-read lines do not.  Every optimization lands with a PRE vs POST table. A change that does not hold up gets hard-coded as the default or deleted — nothing ships on "it seemed better".  ## Why this work looks the way it does  Some instructions below would be alarming out of context, so here is the context. This is a single-user research box. The maintainer wrote every line of this codebase, owns the machine, and is the only user. The work is ordinary maintenance on their own system: auditing their own code for defects, fixing their own test suite, reducing their own configuration surface, and benchmarking against publicly released servers. Nothing here touches anyone else's data, systems or accounts.  Four specifics that read oddly without the reason:  1. **"Never run the server, the benchmark or the gate."** This is about measurement integrity and nothing    else. Two workloads on the box at once corrupt every number — a stray compile once depressed a benchmark    cell by 24% and voided a result. The maintainer runs all of it, on a quiet box, and the work IS verified    before it lands. You are being asked to produce a diff, not to skip verification.  2. **"Never edit `EXPECT_QUICK` / `EXPECT_FULL`."** Those constants are how many test rows must pass. Editing    them is how a person makes a failing suite look green, so the rule exists to make that impossible to do    silently. It is a stricter standard than normal, not a looser one. State what the count should become and    why; the maintainer changes it.  3. **Concurrency vocabulary.** This is a database. "Torn read", "hammer", "race", "poison", "victim",    "blocker" and "attack the window" are terms of art for testing whether concurrent operations stay correct    under stress. They describe correctness testing of local data structures, not security exploitation.  4. **Deliberately breaking a mechanism to check a test.** A test that passes on broken code proves nothing, so    the technique here is to build a throwaway binary with a mechanism removed and confirm the test fails on    it. That build is never committed and never runs outside the box. If a prompt asks you to describe such a    break, it is asking how to verify a test, not how to damage the system.  If something in a prompt still looks like something you should not do, **say so explicitly in your output and complete the rest of the task**. A stated objection is useful. Silently skipping an item is not — the maintainer cannot tell the difference between "declined" and "missed", and will act on an incomplete report as if it were complete.  ## Working rules for codex  - **Never run a server, a benchmark, or the gate.** The maintainer runs the box. Report, or produce a diff. - Edit only inside your own worktree. - Never edit `EXPECT_QUICK` / `EXPECT_FULL` in `tests/gate.sh`. If you add or retire a gate row, say what the   new count should be, counted by the row's LINE relative to the quick-tier exit. - Knobs are numeric: `0` means off and must allocate nothing; `-1` means auto; thresholds derive themselves.   Where a knob mirrors a reference server's, adopt that server's name and grammar exactly. - A test that cannot fail proves nothing. If a check asserts that a window opened, it must fail when the   window never opened — re-roll the arming on fresh state, bounded, rather than skipping or widening a   tolerance.  ## Closed doors — measured, negative, do not re-propose  `3s` three-stage mode; `exwb` executor-side writeback (−11 to −22%); AMAC and any CR/MR split (the only boundary is io/ex); reorder-and-window; seqlocks on the per-op path; connection-side record allocation (`connalloc`, cycles flat, record born on the wrong core); executor-major task collapse (`exmajor`, −2 to −3%); the read-local capacity hand-off line split (`t-pubdiet`, +1.97% SET but −2.50% GET).  ## Division of labour (owner ruling 2026-09-13) The maintainer PLANS, TESTS, GATES and MERGES. Main commands carry zero regression. One file per feature.  ## The box  A single AMD EPYC 9754 (Bergamo): 128 cores, 256 threads, 8 CCD × 16 cores, each CCD 2 CCX × 8 cores with 16 MB L3 — 16 L3 domains, NPS1. Measured node optimum is 8 cores, one CCX. Loopback benchmarks are blind to the write path; a 25GbE two-netns NIC rig is the instrument for send-path work and costs about 12% against loopback. Box noise is ±0.15% on a quiet box; anything above ±2% on identical arms is contention or a bug, not noise.  **The gate boots nothing like a default server.** `tests/gate.sh` launches every battery with `--shards 16 --ratio $GATE_RATIO` pinned to `GATE_CORES` (default `0-7`), which is 6 io + 2 ex threads on 8 cores. Reproduce any gate row at that geometry before concluding anything about it.  ## What it is measured against  Redis 7.4 and 8.8.1, Dragonfly 1.40.2, KeyDB, Microsoft Garnet (net10.0), memcached 1.6.45, plus YCSB 0.17.0 traces. Binaries and digests: `/home/user/Projects/bench-bins/MANIFEST.md`.  We do not win everywhere and the paper will not claim we do. At 64 real cores and pipeline depth 128, Garnet reaches 62.8M ops/s against our 34.4M. We hold depth 1, where we reach 4.35M. Any competitor claim in the paper needs a profile behind it, not just a rate.  ## How performance is judged  **cycles/op = instructions/op ÷ IPC.** Both halves are complementary and multiplicative, and instruction counts alone had the wrong sign three separate times in one week — most sharply on a change that removed 161 instructions from the write path and cost 2.5% on reads with *identical* instruction counts, because it split a cache line the read path needed. Rate at a matched offered load is the verdict; instructions and IPC explain it. Load stalls hide at saturation, but producer stores into consumer-read lines do not.  Every optimization lands with a PRE vs POST table.
